skills.name: Brand identity kit
skills.one_liner: Logo concepts, palette with contrast checks, type pairing and usage rules.
skills.description: Creates a brand identity starter kit: three distinct logo directions generated as concept images and refined, a colour system with WCAG 2.2 contrast pairs, an open-licence type pairing with a scale, usage rules and mock-ups. It is assembled as a guideline page. Concepts are flagged for vector redraw and a trademark check before adoption.
skills.when: a new business, rebrand or new product line needs a look, or the current identity is inconsistent or homemade

inputs.label: Positioning, personality, audience and name
inputs.example: Calm, expert, a little playful; plant shop for first-time plant owners

inputs.label: Current logo, colours, photos or signage
Brands or styles the owner likes and dislikes
Where the identity will live first
inputs.example: Shop sign, Instagram, website, paper bags

outputs.name: Logo concepts and mock-ups
outputs.description: Three directions on light and dark, and the chosen one on sign, avatar, card and site header.

outputs.name: Identity guidelines
outputs.description: Logo usage, clear space, minimum sizes, colours with approved pairs, type scale and don'ts.

outputs.name: Brand guideline one-pager
outputs.description: The essentials on one page.

skills.instructions: 1. Start from the brand platform in memory. If it is missing, run a 20-minute brief with the owner (personality in three words, audience, competitors, feeling to avoid) or pair with positioning work. 2. Audit existing assets and competitors' visual codes with vision_describe, so the identity neither blends in nor clashes. 3. Develop three genuinely distinct concept directions (for example wordmark, symbol plus wordmark, monogram), each with a rationale tied to the brand personality. Generate logo concepts with image_generate (clean and flat, on white and on dark) and iterate with image_edit. Keep a prompt log. 4. Build the colour system: primary, secondary, neutrals and semantic colours. Compute contrast ratios in code_interpreter against WCAG 2.2 (4.5:1 body text, 3:1 large text and UI components) and list approved text and background pairs. 5. Pair a display face and a text face from open-licence libraries, with a type scale and fallback stacks. 6. Write usage rules: clear space, minimum sizes, favicon and avatar crops, logo on photos, and don'ts. 7. After the owner picks a direction, mock it up on a sign, social avatar, business card and website header. 8. Assemble the guideline page with web_page_generate and the one-pager with document_generate. Flag that AI-generated concepts should be redrawn as vector by a designer and checked with trademark-search-prep before adoption. 9. State what could not be verified: font licences beyond the open library, and similarity to existing marks until a trademark search is run.

workflow.brief: Confirm the brief and audit existing and competitor visuals.
workflow.acceptance: Personality, audience and visual codes to avoid are written down.

workflow.acceptance: Three directions, each with rationale and prompt log, clean on light and dark.

workflow.acceptance: Every approved pair meets its WCAG 2.2 ratio.

workflow.acceptance: Choice recorded with any change requests.

workflow.acceptance: Mock-ups on at least four applications; legible at favicon size.

workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; every approved colour pair meets its ratio; the logo is legible at minimum size.

skills.name: Moodboard & creative direction
skills.one_liner: A moodboard and art direction notes that align everyone before production.
skills.description: Aligns everyone on a look before production: mood words, a hex palette, type, and photography and illustration style in two or three directions of original generated images. It adds art-direction notes (light, lens, grading, casting, styling, props) and do/don't pairs, with the owner's own references read for what they like.
skills.when: before a photoshoot, rebrand, website, campaign, packaging or video, or when people disagree about 'the look'

inputs.label: What is being made and for whom
inputs.example: Menu photos and website refresh this summer

inputs.label: The feeling in three to five words, and what to avoid
Photos, screenshots or links the owner likes
Existing brand guidelines

outputs.description: Boards per direction with images, palette swatches, type and mood words.

outputs.description: Original generated images per direction, with a prompt log.

outputs.name: Art-direction notes
outputs.description: Lighting, lens and crop, colour grading, casting and styling, props, graphics and do/don'ts.

skills.instructions: 1. Capture the brief: project, audience, the feeling in three to five words, must-haves, and what it must not feel like. 2. Gather inputs: brand guidelines, the owner's own photos and screenshots (vision_describe says what they like about each), and a few public references by link for internal inspiration only. References are never copied or used in production. 3. Generate 12–20 original images in two or three directions with image_generate, varying lighting, palette, composition and subject styling, and keep a prompt log; add one or two type specimens. 4. Arrange a board per direction with web_page_generate: mood words, hex palette swatches, type and texture. 5. Write art-direction notes: lighting (for example soft window light, high key), lens and crop, colour grading, casting and styling (inclusive representation, no stereotypes), props, graphic elements and motion cues. 6. Add do/don't pairs, using image_edit to show the same shot done right and wrong. 7. The owner picks a direction; refine the board and notes. 8. State what could not be verified: licences for referenced external images, which must not be used in production.

skills.name: Wireframes & user flows
skills.one_liner: Low-fidelity screens and flows that make the interaction testable.
skills.description: Makes low-fidelity wireframes and user flows for the top tasks, content first and mobile first. Every state is included (empty, loading, error, success), with accessibility basics built in. They are built as a clickable canvas prototype with annotations and a five-user hallway test plan, so the interaction is tested before visual design or code.
skills.when: a new feature, booking flow, checkout, app or page is being planned and people need to see and try it before building

inputs.label: Who the users are and the top three tasks
inputs.example: Customers booking a table for a group

inputs.label: Platform, existing system and must-keep elements
Screenshots of what exists today

outputs.description: Greyscale, every top task completable, all states included.

outputs.description: Entry points, steps, decisions, errors and exits.

outputs.name: Annotations and test plan
outputs.description: Behaviours, validation rules, open questions and a five-user test script.

skills.instructions: 1. Define the users, the top three tasks and the success criteria for each; list constraints. Read current screens with vision_describe. 2. Write a user flow per task with diagram_generate: entry points, steps, decisions, errors and exits. 3. Go content first: list the content and actions for each screen in priority order before any layout. 4. Wireframe in greyscale (no brand colours, placeholder imagery), mobile first at the stated breakpoints, including empty, loading, error and success states. 5. Apply usability heuristics as you go (visibility of status, recognition over recall, error prevention) and accessibility basics (focus order, visible labels, targets of at least 24 x 24 CSS px, aiming for 44). 6. Build a clickable low-fi prototype with app_build so every top task can be tried end to end. 7. Annotate behaviours, validation rules and open questions. 8. Write a five-user hallway test plan: tasks, success measures and what to observe. 9. State what could not be verified: assumptions about user behaviour and technical feasibility.

skills.name: Heuristic UX review
skills.one_liner: Evaluate a product against Nielsen's 10 heuristics with severity ratings.
skills.description: Walks the real key journeys on mobile and desktop in the companion browser, stopping before payment or personal data, and evaluates each screen against Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics. Issues are logged with annotated screenshots and 0–4 severity ratings calibrated by a second reviewer, and fixes are ranked by severity and effort.
skills.when: a website or app converts poorly, users get lost, support gets 'how do I' questions, or before a redesign

inputs.label: The site or app to review
The key journeys to walk
inputs.example: Find a class and book it; buy a gift card

inputs.label: Drop-off data by step, if available
What customers complain about

outputs.name: Issue log with severities
outputs.description: Journey, step, heuristic, issue, screenshot, severity 0–4, fix and effort.

outputs.name: UX review report
outputs.description: Top issues with annotated screenshots, quick wins and positives worth keeping.

outputs.name: Annotated screenshots
outputs.description: Each issue marked on the screen where it occurs.

skills.instructions: 1. Agree the key journeys and devices, and pull step drop-off data with connector_read if analytics is connected. 2. Walk each journey in the companion browser at mobile and desktop widths, screenshotting every step. Stop before payment or entering personal data, and never create accounts. 3. Evaluate each screen with vision_describe against Nielsen's 10 heuristics: visibility of system status; match with the real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency; aesthetic and minimalist design; helping users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; help and documentation. 4. Log each issue: journey, step, heuristic, description, evidence screenshot, severity 0–4 (frequency x impact x persistence) and suggested fix. 5. Annotate the screenshots with image_edit to show each problem. 6. Prioritise on a severity-by-effort matrix, quick wins first, and record positives worth keeping. 7. Have a second evaluator calibrate severities. 8. A heuristic review finds likely problems; recommend a usability test to confirm the top ones. 9. State what could not be verified: logged-in areas not reviewed and real user behaviour.

workflow.title: Walk the key journeys
workflow.brief: Walk each journey at two widths and screenshot every step.
workflow.acceptance: Screenshots of every step at two widths; the walk stopped before payment or personal data.

workflow.title: Heuristic evaluation
workflow.brief: Evaluate each screen against the ten heuristics.
workflow.acceptance: Every issue cites a heuristic, step and screenshot.

workflow.title: Annotate evidence
workflow.brief: Mark each issue on its screenshot.
workflow.acceptance: Every logged issue has an annotated image.

workflow.title: Findings report
workflow.brief: Render the issue log and report.
workflow.acceptance: Issues ranked by severity and effort; positives listed.

workflow.title: Second-evaluator calibration
workflow.brief: A second reviewer re-rates severities on a sample.
workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; severity disagreements resolved with reasons.

skills.name: Accessibility audit (WCAG 2.2 AA)
skills.one_liner: Audit pages or documents against WCAG 2.2 AA with fixes by priority.
skills.description: Audits a WCAG-EM sample of pages or documents against WCAG 2.2 AA: automated scans plus manual keyboard, focus, reflow, target-size, form and contrast checks. Every failure is mapped to its success criterion with evidence, impact and fix, and a draft accessibility statement is included. Legal compliance calls are left to counsel.
skills.when: a customer can't use the site, before a launch or redesign, when a buyer asks for accessibility evidence, or on a regular cycle

inputs.label: Site, key journeys or documents to audit
inputs.example: Home, product, cart and checkout; the menu PDF

inputs.label: The site
Complaints or known problems
inputs.example: A screen-reader user can't check out

inputs.label: Repository access for fixes

outputs.name: Accessibility issue log
outputs.description: Page, element, success criterion (number and name), level, evidence, user impact, fix and priority.

outputs.name: WCAG 2.2 AA audit report
outputs.description: Method and sample, summary by POUR principle, top fixes and retest plan.

outputs.name: Accessibility statement draft
outputs.description: Draft statement for the owner and counsel to review.

skills.instructions: 1. Define the scope with a representative sample chosen per WCAG-EM (templates plus complete key journeys) and the target: WCAG 2.2 Level AA. 2. Run automated checks (axe-core or pa11y in the companion shell sandbox) on each sample page and save the output with tool versions. Automated tools catch only part of the issues. 3. Manual checks in the companion browser: keyboard-only navigation (visible focus, logical order, no traps, 2.4.11 focus not obscured), skip links, headings and landmarks, form labels and error handling (3.3.1, 3.3.3), 2.5.8 target size (at least 24 x 24 CSS px), 2.5.7 dragging alternatives, 3.3.8 accessible authentication, 3.2.6 consistent help, 3.3.7 redundant entry, reflow at 320 px, text spacing and 200% zoom. 4. Visual checks: contrast for text and UI components computed in code_interpreter, use of colour alone, and alt-text quality (vision_describe compares the image with its alt text). 5. Media: captions, transcripts and audio-description needs. Documents: check PDF tags, reading order, alt text and language with file_parse. 6. Log each failure: page, element or selector, success criterion number and name, level, evidence (screenshot or snippet), user impact, fix and priority. 7. Report by POUR principle with the top fixes and a retest plan, plus a draft accessibility statement. 8. Legal compliance determinations (for example under the ADA or the European Accessibility Act) are for the owner and counsel. The audit reports findings only and claims no conformance. 9. State what could not be verified: pages outside the sample and testing with real assistive-technology users.

workflow.title: Automated scans
workflow.brief: Run automated accessibility scans on each sample page in the sandbox.
workflow.acceptance: Scan output saved per page with tool name and version.

workflow.title: Manual keyboard and visual checks
workflow.brief: Test keyboard, focus, reflow, target size, forms and authentication on each sample page.
workflow.acceptance: Each sample page has a completed manual checklist with evidence.

workflow.brief: Compute contrast ratios and review alt text and documents.

workflow.title: Findings log and report

workflow.acceptance: Every failure has criterion, evidence, impact, fix and priority.

workflow.title: Criterion mapping check
workflow.brief: Check each failure maps to the correct success criterion.
workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; every failure mapped to the correct WCAG 2.2 criterion with evidence.

quality_checks.criterion: Every failure cites the WCAG 2.2 success criterion number, evidence and fix
Manual keyboard testing is done, not only automated scans
No claim of legal compliance; conformance claims are left to the owner and counsel
The WCAG 2.2 additions (2.4.11, 2.5.7, 2.5.8, 3.2.6, 3.3.7, 3.3.8) are explicitly checked
The sample is chosen per WCAG-EM with a rationale

skills.name: Design system starter
skills.one_liner: Tokens, core components and usage guidelines for consistent UI.
skills.description: Sets up a starter design system from an inventory of the existing UI. It defines tiered design tokens (primitive to semantic, light and dark) exported as JSON and CSS variables, and 10–15 core components with anatomy, variants, states, keyboard behaviour and ARIA notes. It adds usage guidelines, a live HTML reference page and simple governance.
skills.when: the product or site has drifted into many button styles and colours, a developer or agency needs a standard, or before a redesign

inputs.label: Screenshots or URLs of the current product or site
Brand colours, type and logo
Framework and where the tokens will be used
Components used most

outputs.description: Primitive, semantic and component tokens with light and dark modes.

outputs.name: Component reference
outputs.description: Every component and state rendered, with usage notes.

outputs.name: Usage guidelines
outputs.description: When to use what, content rules, do/don'ts, governance and versioning.

skills.instructions: 1. Inventory the existing UI from screenshots and live pages with vision_describe and web_fetch, and count the inconsistencies: colours, font sizes, button styles and spacing values. 2. Define tokens in tiers in code_interpreter: primitives (palette, type scale, spacing on a 4 or 8 px grid, radii, shadows, durations) to semantic tokens (text-primary, surface, border, accent, success, warning, danger) to component tokens, with dark mode. 3. Verify accessibility of the semantic pairs: WCAG 2.2 contrast in both modes, focus-indicator contrast and minimum target size. 4. Specify the core components (button, link, input, select, checkbox and radio, textarea, form field with label, help and error, card, alert, dialog, tabs, table, badge, navigation), each with anatomy, variants, states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, error, loading), keyboard behaviour and ARIA notes. 5. Write usage guidelines: when to use which component, content rules and do/don'ts. 6. Export tokens as Design Tokens Community Group-style JSON and CSS custom properties to workspace_files, and build a live HTML reference page with web_page_generate showing every component and state. 7. Describe governance: how to propose changes, and versioning. 8. State what could not be verified: framework-specific implementation and component behaviour inside the owner's codebase.

skills.description: Designs a batch of on-brand social graphics: four to six reusable templates (quote, tip, announcement, product, event) and ready-to-post images sized for each platform's safe zones. The owner's photos are edited without distorting products or faces. Each graphic comes with captions and alt text, checked for legibility and contrast at phone size.

skills.instructions: 1. Load the brand guidelines (colours, type, logo rules, voice) and the content to feature. 2. Confirm platforms and sizes, and check them against each platform's current help pages. Typical sizes: 1080 x 1350 feed portrait; 1080 x 1920 stories and reels covers, with text kept clear of roughly the top 250 px and bottom 340 px; 1200 x 627 LinkedIn link; 1080 x 1080 square. 3. Design four to six reusable templates with a clear hierarchy (hook headline of eight words or fewer, one supporting line, brand mark) on a grid. 4. skills.name: Infographic & explainer visual
skills.one_liner: Turn a process or data set into one clear, accessible visual.
skills.description: Turns a process, comparison or dataset into one clear visual. It states the takeaway first, verifies the numbers, picks the chart form by the question, and annotates on the chart rather than in a legend. It uses a colour-blind-safe palette with no misleading scales, provides alt text and a data-table equivalent, and exports for web, social and print.
skills.when: numbers or a process need to be understood at a glance: an impact report, a pitch, a social post, a training aid or a sign

inputs.label: What the audience should take away
The data or process description, with sources
Who will see it and where
inputs.example: Donor event, printed and on Instagram

inputs.label: Colours and type

outputs.name: Infographic
outputs.description: Web, social (1080 x 1350) and print-ready vector versions.

outputs.name: Accessible web version with data table
outputs.description: The visual plus a text and table equivalent.

outputs.name: Standalone charts
outputs.description: Individual charts for reuse in decks and reports.

skills.instructions: 1. Write the one-sentence takeaway and audience. If the data doesn't support the takeaway, say so before designing anything. 2. Check the data with file_parse and code_interpreter: source, date, units and denominators; compute any derived numbers and show the working. 3. Choose the form by the question: comparison (bar), change over time (line), part-to-whole (stacked bar, rarely pie), process (flow with diagram_generate), distribution (histogram or dot plot), geography (a map only if location matters). 4. Sketch the hierarchy: the headline is the takeaway; three to five supporting points; annotations on the chart instead of legends; a source line. 5. Build with chart_generate in brand colours with a colour-blind-safe palette, direct labels and zero-based bars, avoiding 3D and dual axes. Use image_generate only for simple illustrative elements, never to represent data. 6. Accessibility: sufficient contrast, text no smaller than about 12 pt in print, alt text that states the takeaway, and a text or table equivalent on the web version built with web_page_generate. 7. Export web (SVG or HTML), social (1080 x 1350) and print (vector) versions, and check legibility of each with vision_describe. 8. Review every number against its source. 9. State what could not be verified: numbers whose original source could not be traced.

workflow.brief: Write the takeaway and check the data's source, units and denominators.
workflow.acceptance: Takeaway written; every data point has a source and date.

workflow.title: Compute figures
workflow.brief: Compute derived figures and show the working.
workflow.acceptance: Derived numbers reproduce from inputs.

workflow.title: Design the visual
workflow.brief: Build charts and layout in brand style.
workflow.acceptance: Headline states the takeaway; direct labels; zero-based bars.

workflow.brief: Check every number and look for misleading scales.
workflow.acceptance: First line is APPROVED or CHANGES; every number matches its source; no misleading scales.

workflow.title: Exports, alt text and text equivalent
workflow.brief: Export sizes and build the accessible web version.
workflow.acceptance: Alt text and a table equivalent exist for every version.

skills.description: Produces a slide deck (PPTX or PDF, or a self-contained HTML deck as a fallback) from an outline: a storyline told by action titles, one idea per slide, evidence shown visually with sourced charts, and speaker notes on every slide, plus optional rehearsal audio of the notes.

skills.instructions: 1. Outline first: the audience, the one decision or belief the deck should produce, and a storyline, either situation, complication, resolution (Minto) or Duarte's what-is against what-could-be. 2. Write 6–12 slide headlines as full-sentence takeaways (action titles) and read them in order; they must tell the story on their own. 3. Keep one idea per slide; keep slide text short and put detail in the speaker notes. 4. Show evidence visually: charts from data with chart_generate (takeaway in the title, source on the slide), diagrams for processes, and generated images with image_generate only where they aid understanding, never as decoration. 5. Build with deck_generate as PPTX (or PDF). If that is unavailable, write one self-contained HTML deck with keyboard navigation using web_page_generate. 6. Apply the brand template or a clean default: body text 24 pt or larger, contrast of at least 4.5:1, alt text on images and a logical reading order. 7. Write speaker notes for every slide: what to say and roughly how long. 8. Optionally render the notes with tts so the owner can hear a rehearsal. 9. Report the file paths, naming every file produced on its own line as 'Artifact: <path relative to the workspace>' via workspace_files. 10. State what could not be verified: numbers in the deck without a traceable source.

skills.name: Packaging concept
skills.one_liner: Packaging directions with dieline notes, hierarchy and shelf-impact checks.
skills.description: Develops two or three packaging directions from a brief and a shelf audit of the category, with an information hierarchy and a three-second read. Concepts are rendered on the pack and placed in a simulated shelf for squint and distance tests. Dieline and print notes, a mandatory-label checklist for a qualified reviewer, and honest sustainability options are included.
skills.when: a product is moving into retail, being relaunched, or looks homemade next to competitors

inputs.label: Product, price point, format and channel
Logo, colours, type and guidelines
Photos of the category shelf or competitor packs
Budget, run size, printer and material limits

outputs.name: Concept renders and shelf simulation
outputs.description: Front and side panels per direction, placed among competitors.

outputs.name: Packaging concept presentation
outputs.description: Brief, shelf audit, directions, tests and recommendation.

outputs.name: Dieline and label checklist
outputs.description: Structure, dimensions to confirm, bleed, safe zone, barcode quiet zone, finishes and mandatory label items to confirm.

skills.instructions: 1. Brief: product, price point, channel (shelf, e-commerce unboxing, marketplace), competitors on shelf, brand assets, format constraints, budget and run size. 2. Shelf audit: gather photos of the category shelf (owner's phone or web) and describe the category codes with vision_describe: what everyone does, and where there is room to stand out. 3. Set the information hierarchy: brand, product name, key benefit or variant, proof and claims, then mandatory information. Define the three-second read. 4. Generate two or three distinct directions as renders on the actual pack format (front and side panels) with image_generate, and use image_edit to place them on the owner's real pack photo where available. 5. Shelf-impact test: place each concept in a simulated shelf image and run squint, three-second and distance legibility checks, plus a colour-blind check on variant colour-coding. 6. Dieline notes: structure (box, pouch, label), dimensions to confirm with the printer, panels, bleed (typically 3 mm or 0.125 in), safe zone, glue flaps, barcode quiet zone, and cost flags for finishes such as foil or embossing. 7. Mandatory label checklist for the relevant rules (for example ingredients, allergens, net quantity, cosmetics INCI list, recycling marks), to be confirmed by a qualified regulatory person. Health and environmental claims ('eco-friendly', 'organic') are flagged for substantiation. 8. Sustainability options: material reduction, mono-material, recycled content, and honest claims only. Present everything with deck_generate. 9. State what could not be verified: printer specifications, material costs and regulatory requirements by market.

workflow.acceptance: Category codes and white space documented with photo evidence.

A preflight proof checks typos, overflow, resolution and QR codes, and a printer spec sheet is included. The owner signs off the proof before anything is ordered.

skills.instructions: 1. Brief: the piece, its purpose and the one action wanted, audience, distribution (hand-out, mail, wall, table), quantity, size and paper, budget and deadline. 2. Write the copy to a hierarchy (headline, benefit, details, call to action, contact or QR) and cut ruthlessly. For menus, apply menu-engineering placement if item data exists. 3. Lay out on a grid with brand assets, using three or four type sizes at most; generate or edit imagery at print resolution with image_generate and image_edit. 4. Apply print specs: final trim size, 3 mm or 0.125 in bleed, safe margin, CMYK colour (rich black for large areas, pure black for small text), images at 300 dpi at final size, fonts embedded or outlined, PDF/X export, and spot colours if used. Check the printer's own requirements with web_search. 5. Accessibility for print: body text 12 pt or larger, high contrast, no text over busy images, and QR codes with a short URL fallback. 6. Preflight the exported PDF with vision_describe for typos, overflow, low-resolution images and QR scannability. 7. The owner signs off the proof via request_owner_decision before anything goes to print. Ordering from a printer spends money and is the owner's step. 8. Write the printer spec sheet. 9. State what could not be verified: colour match on press and printer-specific requirements not published.
